question: What is Section 31A of the NDPS Act and is there a death penalty under the NDPS Act?
answer: Section 31A of the NDPS Act, 1985 provides for enhanced punishment for specified repeat offences involving commercial quantities of designated narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances (or financing or harbouring in relation thereto) after a prior conviction under specified provisions of the Act. While Section 31A originally prescribed a mandatory death penalty, judicial rulings held mandatory death sentences unconstitutional, leading to the NDPS (Amendment) Act, 2014. Under the current statutory text of Section 31A, the court has discretion to sentence a repeat offender either to death or to rigorous imprisonment for 30 years alongside a statutory fine.

question: What is Section 11 and the maximum detention period under the PIT NDPS Act?
answer: Under Section 11 of the PIT NDPS Act, 1988, the general maximum period for which any person may be detained in pursuance of a detention order is 1 year from the date of detention. However, in cases where a declaration has been made under Section 10 of the PIT NDPS Act, 1988 in respect of detention orders relating to highly vulnerable areas, Section 11 provides that the maximum period of preventive detention shall be 2 years from the date of detention.

answer: Under Section 10 of the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988 (PIT NDPS Act, 1988), an officer specially empowered by the Central Government (not below the rank of Joint Secretary) may issue a declaration within five weeks of the detention order in respect of a person who engages or is likely to engage in illicit traffic in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances in areas highly vulnerable to such traffic. answer: Criminal conviction for offences defined under the NDPS Act, 1985 is awarded by a competent court following judicial trial. question: What is the difference between NDPS Act and PIT NDPS Act?
answer:
The NDPS Act, 1985 and the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988 (PIT NDPS Act, 1988) serve distinct legal functions:
* The NDPS Act, 1985 provides for criminal prosecution, judicial trial, and punishment for offences committed under the Act.
* The PIT NDPS Act, 1988 provides for executive preventive detention intended to prevent persons from engaging in illicit traffic in narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, without such detention amounting to a criminal conviction.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 8 Prohibition of Certain Operations
question: What operations are prohibited under Section 8 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Under Section 8 of the NDPS Act, 1985, no person shall:
1. Cultivate any coca plant or gather any portion of coca plant;
2. Cultivate the opium poppy or any cannabis plant; or
3. Produce, manufacture, possess, sell, purchase, transport, warehouse, use, consume, import inter-State, export inter-State, import into India, export from India or tranship any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance.

Exceptions:
These prohibitions do not apply to operations carried out for medical or scientific purposes and in the manner and to the extent provided by the provisions of the Act, Rules, Orders, or terms of any licence, permit, or authorisation issued thereunder. Special provisions also apply to cannabis cultivated exclusively for industrial purposes (obtaining fiber or seed) or for horticultural purposes by general or special order of the Government.

question: What is prohibited under Section 8A of the NDPS Act regarding property derived from an offence?
answer:
Section 8A of the NDPS Act, 1985 prohibits operations in relation to illicitly acquired property derived from drug offences. It provides that no person shall:
1. Convert or transfer any property knowing that such property is derived from an offence committed under the NDPS Act or under the corresponding law of any other country, with the intent of concealing or disguising its illicit origin, or helping any person who is involved in the commission of the offence to evade legal consequences;
2. Conceal or disguise the true nature, source, location, disposition, movement, title with respect to, or ownership of property, knowing that such property is derived from an NDPS offence or corresponding foreign offence; or
3. Knowingly acquire, possess, or use any property which was derived from an offence under the NDPS Act or under corresponding foreign law.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 9A Power to Control and Regulate Controlled Substances
question: What powers does the Central Government have under Section 9A regarding controlled substances and precursor chemicals?
answer:
Under Section 9A of the NDPS Act, 1985, if the Central Government is of the opinion that, having regard to the use of any controlled substance in the production or manufacture of any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance, it is necessary or expedient in the public interest so to do, it may, by order, provide for regulating or prohibiting the production, manufacture, supply, distribution, trade, commerce, possession, and consumption of that controlled substance.

Such orders may require licences, permits, maintenance of records, submission of returns, and labelling (e.g., the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Regulation of Controlled Substances) Order, 2013 covering precursors such as Ephedrine, Pseudoephedrine, Acetic Anhydride, and Anthranilic Acid). Contravention of an order made under Section 9A is punishable under Section 25A with rigorous imprisonment for up to 10 years and a fine up to ₹1,00,000.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 20 Punishment for Contravention in Relation to Cannabis Plant and Cannabis
question: What are the punishments for cannabis offences under Section 20 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 20 of the NDPS Act, 1985 prescribes distinct punishments for contraventions in relation to cannabis plant (cultivation) and cannabis (charas/resin and ganja):

1. **Cultivation of Cannabis Plant (Section 20(a))**:
   * Rigorous imprisonment (RI) for a term which may extend to **10 years**, and a fine which may extend to **₹1,00,000 (one lakh rupees)**.

2. **Production, Manufacture, Possession, Sale, Purchase, Transport, Import/Export inter-State, or Use of Cannabis (Section 20(b))**:
   * **Small Quantity (Section 20(b)(ii)(A))**: Rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to **1 year**, or a fine which may extend to **₹10,000**, or both.
   * **Lesser than Commercial but Greater than Small Quantity (Intermediate Quantity) (Section 20(b)(ii)(B))**: Rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to **10 years**, and a fine which may extend to **₹1,00,000**.
   * **Commercial Quantity (Section 20(b)(ii)(C))**: Rigorous imprisonment for a term which **shall not be less than 10 years but which may extend to 20 years**, and a fine which **shall not be less than ₹1,00,000 but which may extend to ₹2,00,000** (the court may impose a fine exceeding ₹2,00,000 for reasons recorded in the judgment).

*Statutory Weight Thresholds (S.O. 1055(E))*: For Ganja, Small Quantity is 1 kg, Commercial Quantity is 20 kg. For Charas/Hashish, Small Quantity is 100 g, Commercial Quantity is 1 kg.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 21 Punishment for Contravention in Relation to Manufactured Drugs and Preparations
question: What are the penalties under Section 21 of the NDPS Act for manufactured drugs and preparations?
answer:
Section 21 of the NDPS Act, 1985 prescribes quantity-graded punishments for contravention in relation to manufactured drugs (such as Heroin, Smack, Brown Sugar, Morphine, Codeine, Methadone) and any preparation containing them:

1. **Small Quantity (clause (a))**:
   * Rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to **1 year**, or with a fine which may extend to **₹10,000**, or with both.
2. **Intermediate Quantity (clause (b))** (quantity lesser than commercial but greater than small quantity):
   * Rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to **10 years**, and with a fine which may extend to **₹1,00,000**.
3. **Commercial Quantity (clause (c))**:
   * Rigorous imprisonment for a term which **shall not be less than 10 years but which may extend to 20 years**, and a fine which **shall not be less than ₹1,00,000 but which may extend to ₹2,00,000** (the court may impose a fine exceeding ₹2,00,000 for reasons to be recorded in the judgment).

*Note on Mixture Calculation*: Following the Supreme Court Constitution Bench ruling in Hira Singh v. Union of India (2020), in case of seizure of a mixture containing a manufactured drug with neutral substance, the entire weight of the mixture is to be considered for determining small, intermediate, or commercial quantity.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 23 Punishment for Illegal Import into India, Export from India or Transhipment
question: What is the punishment under Section 23 of the NDPS Act for illegal import, export, or transhipment?
answer:
Section 23 of the NDPS Act, 1985 punishes whoever, in contravention of any provision of the Act or any rule or order made or condition of licence or permit granted thereunder, imports into India or exports from India or tranships any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance:

1. **Small Quantity (clause (a))**:
   * Rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to **1 year**, or with fine which may extend to **₹10,000**, or with both.
2. **Intermediate Quantity (clause (b))**:
   * Rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to **10 years**, and with fine which may extend to **₹1,00,000**.
3. **Commercial Quantity (clause (c))**:
   * Rigorous imprisonment for a term which **shall not be less than 10 years but which may extend to 20 years**, and with fine which **shall not be less than ₹1,00,000 but which may extend to ₹2,00,000** (court may impose a fine exceeding ₹2,00,000 for reasons to be recorded in judgment).

This provision targets cross-border smuggling, airport and seaport trafficking, and unauthorized international transit through Indian territory.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 27 Punishment for Consumption of Any Narcotic Drug or Psychotropic Substance
question: What are the statutory punishments for consumption of drugs under Section 27 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 27 of the NDPS Act, 1985 punishes the consumption of any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance:

1. **Specified Hard Drugs (clause (a))**:
   * Where the substance consumed is **cocaine, morphine, diacetylmorphine (heroin)**, or any other narcotic drug or psychotropic substance specified in this behalf by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette:
   * Punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to **1 year**, or with fine which may extend to **₹20,000**, or with both.

2. **Other Drugs or Substances (clause (b))**:
   * Where the substance consumed is other than those specified in clause (a) (e.g., cannabis/ganja or other unlisted psychotropic substances):
   * Punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to **6 months**, or with fine which may extend to **₹10,000**, or with both.

*Immunity Provision*: Under Section 64A of the Act, an addict charged with consumption under Section 27 (or offences involving small quantity) who voluntarily seeks medical treatment for de-addiction in a hospital or institution recognized by the Government may be granted immunity from prosecution.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 27A Punishment for Financing Illicit Traffic and Harbouring Offenders
question: What constitutes an offence and what is the punishment under Section 27A of the NDPS Act for financing illicit traffic or harbouring offenders?
answer:
Under Section 27A of the NDPS Act, 1985, whoever indulges in financing, directly or indirectly, any of the illicit traffic activities specified in sub-clauses (i) to (v) of clause (viiia) of Section 2, or harbours any person engaged in any of those activities, shall be punishable with:

* **Rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 10 years but which may extend to 20 years**, and
* **A fine which shall not be less than ₹1,00,000 (one lakh rupees) but which may extend to ₹2,00,000 (two lakh rupees)**.
* The court may, for reasons to be recorded in the judgment, impose a fine exceeding two lakh rupees.

Key Scope:
1. **Financing illicit traffic**: Providing funds, banking facilities, hawala transfers, cryptocurrency, cash, or credit to facilitate illicit cultivation, production, manufacture, possession, sale, transport, import, or export of narcotic drugs.
2. **Harbouring**: Supplying a person engaged in illicit traffic with shelter, food, drink, money, clothes, arms, ammunition, or means of conveyance, or assisting that person in evading apprehension.
3. **Bail Restrictions**: Section 27A is expressly subject to the strict statutory bar on bail under Section 37.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 29 Punishment for Abetment and Criminal Conspiracy
question: How are abetment and criminal conspiracy punished under Section 29 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 29 of the NDPS Act, 1985 governs abetment and criminal conspiracy in drug offences:

1. **Sub-section (1)**: Whoever abets, or is a party to a criminal conspiracy to commit, an offence punishable under Chapter IV, shall, **whether such offence be or be not committed in consequence of such abetment or in pursuance of such criminal conspiracy**, and notwithstanding anything contained in Section 116 of the Indian Penal Code (or Section 49 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023), be punishable with the punishment provided for that offence.

2. **Sub-section (2)**: A person abets, or is a party to a criminal conspiracy to commit, an offence punishable under this Chapter when in India he abets or conspires to the commission of any act in any place outside India which, if committed in India, would constitute an offence, or vice versa.

*Critical Legal Feature*: Unlike general criminal law under the Penal Code, under Section 29 of the NDPS Act the conspirator or abettor faces the **same full penalty** as the principal offender even if the contemplated drug transaction is intercepted or not completed.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 31 Enhanced Punishment for Offences after Previous Conviction
question: What enhanced punishment applies to repeat offenders under Section 31 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 31 of the NDPS Act, 1985 prescribes enhanced punishment for persons convicted of repeat offences:

1. **Scope**:
   If any person who has been convicted of an offence punishable under Section 19, 24, 27A, or for offences involving commercial quantity of any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance, is subsequently convicted of such an offence under this Act, he shall be punishable for the subsequent offence with:
   * **Imprisonment for a term which may extend to one and one-half times of the maximum term of imprisonment**, and
   * **Fine which may extend to one and one-half times of the maximum amount of fine**.

2. **Minimum Sentence Enhancement**:
   Where a minimum term of imprisonment or minimum fine is prescribed for the subsequent offence, the minimum term of imprisonment shall not be less than one and one-half times of the minimum term, and the minimum fine shall not be less than one and one-half times of the minimum fine (e.g., a 10-year minimum becomes a 15-year minimum, and a ₹1,00,000 fine becomes ₹1,50,000 minimum).

*Distinction*: Section 31 applies to enhanced terms of imprisonment and fines. By contrast, Section 31A governs discretionary capital punishment / 30-year sentence for specific commercial repeat offences.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 35 Presumption of Culpable Mental State
question: What is the statutory presumption of culpable mental state under Section 35 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 35 of the NDPS Act, 1985 creates a statutory reverse burden of proof regarding mens rea in NDPS prosecutions:

1. **Sub-section (1)**: In any prosecution for an offence under this Act which requires a culpable mental state of the accused, the Court **shall presume the existence of such mental state**, but it shall be a defence for the accused to prove the fact that he had no such mental state with respect to the act charged as an offence in that prosecution.

2. **Definition of Culpable Mental State (Explanation to Section 35)**: "Culpable mental state" includes intention, motive, knowledge of a fact, and belief in, or reason to believe, a fact.

3. **Standard of Proof for Defence (Sub-section (2))**: A fact is said to be proved only when the court believes it to exist **beyond a reasonable doubt** and not merely when its existence is established by a preponderance of probability.

*Judicial Prerequisite*: As held by the Supreme Court in Noor Aga v. State of Punjab (2008) and Hanif Khan v. Central Bureau of Narcotics (2020), the prosecution must first establish foundational facts (conscious possession or physical recovery) beyond reasonable doubt before the statutory presumption under Section 35 can be invoked against the accused.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 36 Constitution of Special Courts
question: How are Special Courts constituted and who can preside under Section 36 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 36 of the NDPS Act, 1985 empowers the Government to constitute Special Courts for speedy trial of offences:

1. **Power to Constitute (Sub-section (1))**: The Government may, for the purpose of providing speedy trial of offences under this Act, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute as many Special Courts as may be necessary for such area or areas as may be specified in the notification.

2. **Composition and Qualifications (Sub-section (2) & (3))**:
   * A Special Court shall consist of a single Judge who shall be appointed by the Government with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court.
   * A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a Judge of a Special Court unless he was, immediately before such appointment, a **Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge**.

3. **Jurisdiction**: Special Courts exercise all the powers of a Court of Session and can take cognizance of offences without the accused being committed to it for trial upon perusal of a police report or complaint filed by an authorized officer.

Question: How are Special Courts constituted and who can preside under Section 36 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
Answer: Under Section 36, the Government may constitute Special Courts for the speedy trial of NDPS offences. Each Special Court consists of a single judge who must be a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge, appointed with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 36A Offences Triable by Special Courts and Extended Investigation Timelines
question: Which offences are triable by Special Courts and what are the investigation timelines under Section 36A of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 36A of the NDPS Act, 1985 defines the trial jurisdiction of Special Courts and modifies the standard Code of Criminal Procedure / BNSS investigation timelines:

1. **Trial Jurisdiction (Section 36A(1)(a))**:
   * All offences under the NDPS Act punishable with imprisonment for a term of **more than 3 years** shall be triable exclusively by the Special Court constituted for the area.
   * Offences punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years may be tried summarily or by a Magistrate under Section 36A(5).

2. **Direct Cognizance (Section 36A(1)(d))**:
   * A Special Court may, upon perusal of police report or upon a complaint made by an officer of the Central Government or State Government authorized under this Act, take cognizance of that offence without the accused being committed to it for trial.

3. **Investigation Timelines & Detention Period (Section 36A(4))**:
   * For offences punishable under Section 19, Section 24, Section 27A, or offences involving commercial quantity, Section 167(2) of CrPC (Section 187 BNSS) is modified:
   * The default period for completion of investigation and filing of chargesheet is **180 days** (instead of 90 days).
   * If investigation cannot be completed within 180 days, the Special Court may extend the period **up to 1 year**, upon the report of the Public Prosecutor indicating the progress of the investigation and the specific reasons for the detention of the accused beyond 180 days.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 37 Offences to be Cognizable and Non-Bailable (Twin Conditions for Bail)
question: What are the twin conditions for granting bail under Section 37 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 37 of the NDPS Act, 1985 establishes rigorous statutory hurdles for the grant of bail:

1. **Cognizable and Non-Bailable (Sub-section (1)(a))**:
   * Every offence punishable under the NDPS Act shall be **cognizable**.
   * No person accused of an offence punishable under **Section 19 (embezzlement by licensed cultivator), Section 24 (external dealings), Section 27A (financing illicit traffic & harbouring)**, or for offences involving **commercial quantity** of any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance, shall be released on bail or on his own bond unless:

2. **The Twin Conditions for Bail (Sub-section (1)(b))**:
   * **Condition 1**: The Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application for such release; and
   * **Condition 2**: Where the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the Court is satisfied that there are **reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail**.

3. **Cumulative Application (Sub-section (2))**:
   * The limitations on granting bail specified in Section 37(1)(b) are **in addition to** the limitations under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (or Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) or any other law for the time being in force.

*Judicial Precedent*: The Supreme Court has repeatedly held (e.g., Union of India v. Shiv Shanker Kesari, State of Kerala v. Rajesh) that "reasonable grounds" means something more than a prima facie case; the court must record substantial reasons based on credible material before granting bail in commercial quantity cases.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 41 Power to Issue Warrant and Authorisation
question: Who is empowered to issue search warrants and authorisations under Section 41 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 41 of the NDPS Act, 1985 distributes search and arrest authorization powers between judicial magistrates and empowered gazetted executive officers:

1. **Magisterial Warrants (Section 41(1))**:
   * A Metropolitan Magistrate, a Judicial Magistrate of the first class, or any Magistrate of the second class specially empowered by the State Government in this behalf, may issue a warrant for the arrest of any person whom he has reason to believe to have committed any offence punishable under Chapter IV, or for the search of any building, conveyance or place in which he has reason to believe any narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, controlled substance, or incriminating document/article is kept or concealed.

2. **Authorisation by Gazetted Officers (Section 41(2))**:
   * Any officer of gazetted rank of the Central Excise, Narcotics, Customs, Revenue Intelligence, or any other department of the Central Government, or of the Revenue, Drugs Control, Excise, Police, or other department of a State Government, empowered in this behalf by general or special order of the Central Government or State Government;
   * If he has **reason to believe from personal knowledge or information given by any person and taken down in writing**;
   * May authorize any officer subordinate to him but **superior in rank to a peon, sepoy, or a constable** to arrest such person or search a building, conveyance, or place.

3. **Direct Exercise of Powers (Section 41(3))**:
   * An officer to whom a warrant or authorisation is addressed under Section 41 may search, seize contraband, and arrest suspects with all the powers of an officer acting under Section 42.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 42 Power of Entry, Search, Seizure and Arrest Without Warrant or Authorisation
question: What are the mandatory requirements for entry, search, seizure, and arrest without warrant under Section 42 of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 42 of the NDPS Act, 1985 governs warrantless search and seizure in private places and imposes strict procedural safeguards:

1. **Empowered Officers (Section 42(1))**:
   * Empowerment is derived from specific Central or State Government Notifications, NOT from rank alone. While the Act mentions officers superior in rank to a peon/constable, actual statutory authority to conduct a search under Section 42 must be verified via the applicable notification.

2. **Reason to Believe and Recording Information**:
   * The empowered officer must record secret information or grounds of belief in writing (GD entry/Memo) prior to entry.

3. **Sunset to Sunrise Proviso (Night Searches)**:
   * Recording of grounds of belief is mandatory before entry during night hours if obtaining a warrant is impracticable.

4. **72-Hour Reporting (Section 42(2))**:
   * A copy of the written record must be sent to the immediate superior within 72 hours.

*Legal Audit Note*: Never assume SI/ASI is automatically empowered without verifying the specific designation in the relevant Govt Notification.

Under Section 42(2), a copy of the recorded information/grounds must be sent to the immediate official superior within 72 hours.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 43 Power of Seizure and Arrest in Public Place
question: What are the powers of seizure and arrest in a public place under Section 43 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Section 43 of the NDPS Act, 1985 empowers officers to effect search, seizure, and arrest in public places and transit:

1. **Power to Seize and Arrest**:
   * Any officer of any of the departments mentioned in Section 42 may:
     * Seize in any public place or in transit any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance or controlled substance in respect of which an offence has been committed, along with any animal or conveyance used in carrying it;
     * Detain and search any person whom he has reason to believe to have committed an offence under Chapter IV, and arrest him and any other person in his company.

2. **Definition of Public Place (Explanation to Section 43)**:
   * "Public place" includes any public conveyance, hotel, shop, or any other place intended for use by, or accessible to, the public.

3. **Critical Distinction between Section 42 and Section 43**:
   * As held by the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh and Directorate of Revenue Intelligence v. Premlata (2024), **Section 43 does not require recording information in writing prior to search, nor does it require sending a copy to an official superior within 72 hours**.
   * Section 42 applies to private buildings, conveyances, and enclosed private places; Section 43 applies to public spaces, open roads, and conveyances in transit in public areas.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 50 Conditions Under Which Search of Persons Shall be Conducted
question: What are the mandatory conditions and legal safeguards for conducting personal search under Section 50 of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 50 of the NDPS Act, 1985 provides mandatory statutory safeguards when searching a suspect's bodily person:

1. **Option to be Searched Before Gazetted Officer or Magistrate (Section 50(1))**:
   * When an empowered officer is about to search any person under Section 41, 42, or 43, he shall, **if such person so requires, take such person without unnecessary delay to the nearest Gazetted Officer of any of the departments mentioned in Section 42 or to the nearest Magistrate**.
   * The suspect must be informed of this statutory right clearly (communicating this right in writing or orally with signed acknowledgement is standard practice).

2. **Discretion of the Requisite Authority (Section 50(2) & (3))**:
   * If requisitioned, the Gazetted Officer or Magistrate may discharge the person if no reasonable ground of suspicion is found, or direct that search be made.

3. **Search of Female Persons (Section 50(4))**:
   * **No female shall be searched by anyone excepting a female**.

4. **Emergency Exception (Section 50(5) & (6))**:
   * If it is not possible to take the person to a Gazetted Officer or Magistrate without the possibility of the person parting with possession of the contraband, the officer may proceed with the search, but must record reasons in writing and forward a copy to his immediate official superior within 72 hours.

5. **Applicability Constraint (Physical Body Only)**:
   * As settled by the Supreme Court Constitution Benches in State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh (1999) and Vijaysinh Chandubha Jadeja (2011), Section 50 applies **strictly and exclusively to personal searches of the human body and clothing worn**. It does NOT apply to searches of bags, luggage, containers, premises, or motor vehicles.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 52 Disposal of Persons Arrested and Articles Seized
question: What is the procedure for disposal of arrested persons and seized articles under Section 52 of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 52 of the NDPS Act, 1985 prescribes the initial statutory custody and forwarding procedures upon arrest and seizure:

1. **Informing Grounds of Arrest (Section 52(1))**:
   * Any officer arresting a person under Section 41, Section 42, Section 43 or Section 44 shall, **as soon may be, inform him of the full grounds for such arrest** (fulfilling Article 22(1) of the Constitution).

2. **Disposal under Warrant (Section 52(2))**:
   * Every person arrested and article seized under a warrant issued under sub-section (1) of Section 41 shall be forwarded without unnecessary delay to the Magistrate by whom the warrant was issued.

3. **Disposal without Warrant (Section 52(3))**:
   * Every person arrested and article seized under Section 41(2), Section 42, Section 43 or Section 44 shall be forwarded without unnecessary delay to:
     * (a) The **officer-in-charge of the nearest police station**; or
     * (b) The **officer empowered under Section 53** (investigating officer invested with police station in-charge powers).

4. **Duty of Receiving Officer (Section 52(4))**:
   * The officer receiving the custody of arrested persons and seized articles must take immediate steps to produce them before a Magistrate and take custody of articles in the police station malkhana.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 52A Disposal of Seized Narcotic Drugs and Pre-Trial Sampling Before Magistrate
question: What is the mandatory procedure for inventory certification, sampling, and disposal under Section 52A of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 52A of the NDPS Act, 1985 provides the statutory framework for pre-trial disposal of seized contraband and sampling under magisterial supervision:

1. **Government Notification for Disposal (Section 52A(1))**:
   * The Central Government may specify by notification the narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, or conveyances which shall, having regard to hazardous nature, vulnerability to theft, or lack of storage space, be disposed of by an officer.

2. **Inventory Preparation & Application to Magistrate (Section 52A(2))**:
   * Where any contraband has been seized and forwarded under Section 52(3) or (4), the officer-in-charge shall prepare an inventory of such drugs containing details like description, quality, quantity, mark, numbers, country of origin, and packing;
   * He shall make an application to any Magistrate for the purpose of:
     * (a) **Certifying the correctness of the inventory** so prepared;
     * (b) **Taking photographs** of such drugs or substances in the presence of the Magistrate and certifying such photographs as true; or
     * (c) **Allowing him to draw representative samples of such drugs in the presence of such Magistrate and certifying the correctness of any list of samples so drawn**.

3. **Primary Evidence Status (Section 52A(4))**:
   * Notwithstanding anything contained in the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (or Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023), every court trying an offence shall treat the inventory, the photographs of the drugs, and any list of samples certified by the Magistrate as **primary evidence** in respect of such offence.

*Supreme Court Landmark Rulings*: In Union of India v. Mohan Lal (2016) and Mangilal v. State of MP (2023), the Supreme Court ruled that **samples MUST be drawn in the presence and under the certification of the Magistrate under Section 52A**. Samples drawn at the spot of seizure without Magisterial supervision do not constitute primary evidence.

Under Section 52A(4), the Magisterially certified inventory, photos, and sample list constitute primary evidence in trial.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 53 Power to Invest Officers of Certain Departments with Powers of Officer-in-Charge of Police Station
question: What powers are conferred under Section 53 of the NDPS Act, 1985 and can statements before them be used as confessions?
answer:
Section 53 of the NDPS Act, 1985 enables specialized departmental officers to investigate NDPS crimes:

1. **Conferral of Police Powers (Section 53(1) & (2))**:
   * The Central Government or State Government may, by general or special order, invest any officer of the department of narcotics, customs, central excise, revenue intelligence, or any other department with the powers of an **officer-in-charge of a police station for the investigation of offences under this Act**.

2. **Scope of Investigation Powers**:
   * Officers empowered under Section 53 can summon witnesses, examine suspects, conduct raids, seize illicit property, and file formal complaints/reports before Special Courts.

3. **Legal Status of Statements (Tofan Singh Landmark Ruling)**:
   * In the landmark Constitution Bench judgment of *Tofan Singh v. State of Tamil Nadu (2021) 4 SCC 1*, the Supreme Court held that officers invested with powers under Section 53 are **police officers within the meaning of Section 25 of the Evidence Act (Section 23(1) BSA, 2023)**.
   * Consequently, **any confessional statement made to an officer empowered under Section 53 (including NCB, DRI, Customs, or Excise officers) is inadmissible in evidence** and cannot be used to convict an accused in the absence of independent corroborating evidence.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 55 Police to Take Charge of Articles Seized and Delivered
question: What are the Station House Officer's duties under Section 55 of the NDPS Act regarding custody and sealing of seized contraband?
answer:
Section 55 of the NDPS Act, 1985 governs the safe custody and resealing of seized case property:

1. **Statutory Obligation of Police Station In-charge**:
   * An officer-in-charge of a police station (SHO) shall take charge of and keep in safe custody, pending the orders of the Magistrate, all articles seized under this Act within the local area of that police station and which may be delivered to him.

2. **Affixing Station Seal (Resealing)**:
   * The officer-in-charge shall affix his own seal to such articles;
   * He shall permit any officer who may accompany such articles to the police station or who may be deputed for the purpose, to affix his seal to the articles or to take samples of and from them and all samples so taken shall also be sealed with a seal of the officer-in-charge.

3. **Malkhana Register Entries**:
   * The handed-over articles must be entered into the Malkhana Register (Register No. 19 / Case Property Register) recording seal impressions, exact weights, package descriptions, and signatures of both the seizing officer and the Malkhana in-charge (MHC), maintaining an unbroken chain of custody.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 57 Report of Arrest and Seizure Within Forty-Eight Hours
question: What is the statutory timeline and requirement for reporting arrest and seizure under Section 57 of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 57 of the NDPS Act, 1985 mandates immediate supervisory reporting following an arrest or seizure:

1. **Statutory Obligation**:
   * Whenever any person makes any arrest or seizure under this Act, he shall, **within forty-eight hours (48 hours)** next after such arrest or seizure, make a full report of all the particulars of such arrest or seizure to his **immediate official superior**.

2. **Distinction from Section 42(2) & Section 57A**:
   * **Section 42(2)** requires recording information received or grounds for night search prior to search, and sending a copy to the superior within **72 hours**.
   * **Section 57** requires a comprehensive post-operation report of the completed arrest and seizure within **48 hours**.
   * **Section 57A** (under Chapter VA) requires reporting illegally acquired property identified during financial investigation to the designated authority within 48 hours.

3. **Legal Status of Section 57**:
   * The Supreme Court in *State of Punjab v. Balbir Singh (1994)* and *Gurbax Singh v. State of Haryana (2001)* held that Section 57 is directory in nature; however, investigating officers must not arbitrarily ignore it, as unexplained non-compliance may raise doubt about the bona fides of the seizure.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 60 Liability of Illicit Drugs, Substances, Plants, Articles and Conveyances to Confiscation
question: Under what conditions are illicit drugs, containers, and conveyances liable to confiscation under Section 60 of the NDPS Act, and what is the innocent owner defence?
answer:
Section 60 of the NDPS Act, 1985 provides for the confiscation of contraband, packaging, and conveyances used in drug trafficking:

1. **Contraband and Plants (Section 60(1))**:
   * Whenever any offence punishable under this Act has been committed, the narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, controlled substance, opium poppy, coca bush, or cannabis plant in connection with which or by means of which such offence has been committed, shall be liable to confiscation.

2. **Packages and Coverings (Section 60(2))**:
   * Any package, covering, or receptacle in which any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance is found, and any other contents of such package or covering, shall also be liable to confiscation.

3. **Conveyances and Animals (Section 60(3))**:
   * Any animal or conveyance (motor vehicle, truck, bus, boat, vessel, or aircraft) used in carrying any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance, or any item liable to confiscation under sub-section (1) or (2), shall be liable to confiscation.

4. **The Innocent Owner Defence (Proviso to Section 60(3))**:
   * A conveyance shall **not be confiscated** if the owner of the conveyance proves that it was so used **without the knowledge or connivance of the owner himself, his agent, if any, and the person in charge of the animal or conveyance, and that each of them had taken all reasonable precautions against such use**.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 61 Confiscation of Goods Used for Concealing Illicit Drugs or Substances
question: When are goods used for concealing illicit drugs liable to confiscation under Section 61 of the NDPS Act, 1985?
answer:
Under Section 61 of the NDPS Act, 1985, any goods used for concealing any narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, or controlled substance which is liable to confiscation under the Act, shall also be liable to confiscation.

Scope and Application:
* This provision applies to legitimate commercial cargo, merchandise, agricultural produce, food containers, machine components, false cavities, or luggage used to hide, camoflauge, or conceal illicit narcotics.
* Whether the goods are mixed together with the contraband or used as an outer concealing layer, the concealing goods are forfeited to prevent traffickers from using commercial cover.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 62 Confiscation of Sale Proceeds of Illicit Drugs or Substances
question: When can sale proceeds of illicit drugs be confiscated under Section 62 of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 62 of the NDPS Act, 1985 provides for the confiscation of monetary proceeds generated from illicit drug sales:

* **Statutory Text**: Where any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance is sold by a person having knowledge or reason to believe that the drug or substance is liable to confiscation under this Act, the **sale proceeds thereof shall be liable to confiscation**.

* **Application**:
  * Cash recovered from drug peddlers, bank account funds directly traceable to a drug transaction, hawala payments, or monetary consideration paid by an undercover decoy buyer during a controlled delivery or trap operation are subject to confiscation under Section 62 alongside criminal conviction of the accused.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 63 Procedure in Making Confiscations
question: What is the statutory procedure for ordering confiscation under Section 63 of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 63 of the NDPS Act, 1985 defines the procedure for ordering confiscation by courts or magistrates:

1. **In Trial Before Special Court (Section 63(1))**:
   * In the trial of offences under this Act, whether the accused is **convicted or acquitted or discharged**, the Court shall decide whether any article or thing seized under this Act is liable to confiscation under Section 60 or Section 61 or Section 62, and, if it decides that the thing is so liable, the Court may order confiscation accordingly.

2. **Where Offender is Unknown or Cannot be Found (Section 63(2))**:
   * Where any article or thing is seized under this Act and the accused is not known or cannot be found, the Court or Magistrate may, after an inquiry, order confiscation:
   * **Proviso (Mandatory One-Month Notice)**: No order of confiscation of an article or thing shall be made until the expiration of **one month** from the date of seizing that article or thing, or without hearing any person who may claim any right thereto and the evidence, if any, which he produces in respect of his claim.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Chapter VA Section 68A Application of Forfeiture Provisions
question: To whom does Chapter VA (Forfeiture of Illegally Acquired Property) apply under Section 68A of the NDPS Act?
answer:
Section 68A of the NDPS Act, 1985 defines the categories of persons subject to Chapter VA forfeiture:

1. **Convicted Persons (Section 68A(2)(a))**:
   * Every person who has been convicted of an offence punishable under the NDPS Act with imprisonment for a term of **ten years or more**.

2. **Preventive Detenus under PIT NDPS Act (Section 68A(2)(b))**:
   * Every person in respect of whom an order of detention has been made under the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988 (PIT NDPS Act) or Jammu and Kashmir Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988:
   * Provided that such order of detention has not been revoked on the report of the Advisory Board or set aside by a court of competent jurisdiction.

3. **Relatives and Associates (Section 68A(2)(c) & (d))**:
   * Every person who is a **relative** (spouse, siblings, lineal ascendants, lineal descendants, and spouses of siblings/descendants) of a person referred to in clause (a) or clause (b);
   * Every **associate** (business partner, employer, employee, agent, trustee, or company where 20% or more voting power is held);
   * Any holder of any property which was at any time previously held by a person referred to in clause (a) or (b) unless acquired for adequate consideration in good faith.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Sections 68C and 68E Prohibition of Holding and Tracing Illegally Acquired Property
question: What is prohibited under Section 68C and how is illegally acquired property traced and identified under Section 68E?
answer:
Sections 68C and 68E of the NDPS Act, 1985 establish the prohibition on holding illicit assets and the statutory tracing procedure:

1. **Prohibition of Holding Illegally Acquired Property (Section 68C)**:
   * (1) It shall not be lawful for any person to whom Chapter VA applies to hold any illegally acquired property either by himself or through any other person on his behalf.
   * (2) Where any person holds any illegally acquired property in contravention of sub-section (1), such property shall be liable to be forfeited to the Central Government in accordance with the provisions of Chapter VA.

2. **Identifying Illegally Acquired Property (Section 68E)**:
   * An officer not below the rank of **Inspector of Police** (or officer of equivalent rank in NCB, Customs, Central Excise, or State Excise), on receipt of information or upon conducting financial investigation under Section 57A, shall take all necessary steps to trace and identify any property:
     * He may examine books of account, bank records, land registries, and assets;
     * He records reasons in writing regarding suspicion of illicit origin;
     * Once identified, the officer takes action to seize or freeze the property under Section 68F.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Section 68F Seizure or Freezing of Illegally Acquired Property and 30-Day Confirmation
question: What is the procedure for seizure or freezing of property under Section 68F of the NDPS Act and what is the 30-day confirmation rule?
answer:
Section 68F of the NDPS Act, 1985 provides for the immediate provisional attachment, seizure, or freezing of illicitly acquired assets:

1. **Order of Seizure or Freezing (Section 68F(1))**:
   * Where any officer conducting an inquiry or investigation under Section 68E has reason to believe that any property is illegally acquired property and that such property is likely to be concealed, transferred, or dealt with in any manner which will result in frustrating any proceeding relating to forfeiture, he may make an order seizing such property;
   * Where it is not practicable to seize such property (such as real estate, immovable buildings, or bank accounts), he may make an order that such property shall not be transferred or otherwise dealt with except with prior permission (**Freezing Order**).

2. **48-Hour Notice to Competent Authority (Section 68F(1) Proviso)**:
   * A copy of such order of seizure or freezing shall be served on the person concerned and **within forty-eight hours (48 hours)** be sent to the **Competent Authority** appointed under Section 68D.

3. **30-Day Confirmation Rule (Section 68F(2))**:
   * A freezing order made under sub-section (1) **shall have no effect unless it is confirmed by an order of the Competent Authority within a period of thirty days (30 days)** of its being made.
   * If the Competent Authority does not confirm the freezing order within 30 days, the freezing order automatically lapses by operation of law.

title: NDPS Act, 1985 — Sections 68H and 68-I Notice and Order of Forfeiture of Illegally Acquired Property
question: What is the procedure for notice of forfeiture under Section 68H, final forfeiture under Section 68-I, and who bears the burden of proof under Section 68J?
answer:
Sections 68H, 68-I, and 68J of the NDPS Act, 1985 govern the quasi-judicial forfeiture of property before the Competent Authority:

1. **Show Cause Notice of Forfeiture (Section 68H)**:
   * If the Competent Authority has reason to believe (based on information from investigating officers or other agencies) that any property is illegally acquired property, it shall issue a notice to the person calling upon him within **thirty days** to indicate the sources of his income, earnings, or assets out of which he acquired such property, and to show cause why such property should not be declared illegally acquired and forfeited to the Central Government.

2. **Order of Forfeiture (Section 68-I)**:
   * The Competent Authority, after considering the explanation to the show cause notice and giving the person a reasonable opportunity of being heard, shall record a finding whether the properties are illegally acquired;
   * If satisfied that the properties are illegally acquired, it shall declare by order that such properties stand **forfeited to the Central Government free from all encumbrances**.

3. **Burden of Proof (Section 68J)**:
   * In any forfeiture proceeding under Chapter VA, the **burden of proving that any property is not illegally acquired property shall be on the person affected** (the owner/holder). The agency does not have to disprove the lawful source; the holder must establish the legitimate origin of funds used to purchase the property.

title: NDPS Rules, 1985 — Framework for Regulated Manufacture, Possession, Transport, and Licences
question: What is the regulatory framework under the NDPS Rules, 1985 for legal manufacture, transport, and import/export of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances?
answer:
The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Rules, 1985 (framed under Section 9 and Section 76 of the NDPS Act, 1985) establish the comprehensive licensing and permit regime in India:

1. **Opium Poppy Cultivation & Opium Production (Chapters III & IV)**:
   * Opium poppy cultivation is strictly restricted to designated tracts in Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh under annual licences issued by the Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN) under the Narcotics Commissioner of India.
   * Cultivators must deliver all raw opium harvested to the Central Government Opium Factories (at Ghazipur and Neemuch).

2. **Manufacture and Sale of Manufactured Drugs (Chapter V)**:
   * Manufacture of manufactured drugs (morphine, codeine, thebaine) is prohibited except by licensed pharmaceutical manufacturers possessing quota allocations from the Narcotics Commissioner.

3. **Import and Export Requirements (Chapter VI)**:
   * International trade requires an official **Import Certificate** issued by the Narcotics Commissioner of India and a corresponding **Export Authorisation** issued by the exporting nation's competent authority in compliance with the 1961 Single Convention and 1971 Psychotropic Convention.

4. **Controlled Substances Licencing**:
   * Transport, consignment notes (Form 6 / consignor-consignee declaration), and consignment monitoring are enforced to prevent diversion into illicit channels.

title: NDPS Seizure, Storage, Sampling and Disposal Rules, 2022 — Mandatory Sampling and Storage Procedures
question: What are the mandatory sampling quantities, storage guidelines, and test memo procedures under the NDPS Seizure, Storage, Sampling and Disposal Rules, 2022?
answer:
The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Seizure, Storage, Sampling and Disposal) Rules, 2022 (notified vide G.S.R. 899(E) dated 23.12.2022) establish strict standard operating procedures under Section 52A of the Act:

1. **Sampling Quantity Standards (Rule 10)**:
   * For **Opium, Ganja, and Charas (cannabis resin)**: Samples must be drawn in **duplicate**, each sample weighing not less than **24 grams**.
   * For **all other narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances** (including Heroin, Cocaine, MDMA, Amphetamine, Psychotropic Tablets): Samples must be drawn in **duplicate**, each sample weighing not less than **5 grams**.

2. **Magisterial Supervision (Rule 8 & 9)**:
   * Drawing of representative samples MUST be conducted before the Magistrate upon an application filed under Section 52A(2). Spot sampling at the site of recovery is superseded by the magisterial procedure.

3. **Test Memo and Dispatch to Forensic Laboratory (Rule 11)**:
   * Samples must be dispatched to the designated Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL/CRCL) accompanied by **Test Memo in Form 6** within **seventy-two hours (72 hours)** of drawing samples before the Magistrate.

4. **Storage in Malkhana (Rule 6 & 7)**:
   * Case property must be stored in a dedicated strong room or Malkhana inside a **double-lock trunk/safe** with separate keys kept by the Malkhana In-Charge and the Gazetted Supervisory Officer, subject to mandatory bi-monthly inspections.

title: Ministry of Finance Notification S.O. 1055(E) — Official Small and Commercial Quantity Weight Thresholds
question: What are the official statutory weight thresholds for small quantity and commercial quantity under Notification S.O. 1055(E)?
answer:
Notification S.O. 1055(E) dated 19.10.2001 (as amended) issued by the Ministry of Finance pursuant to clauses (viia) and (xxiiia) of Section 2 of the NDPS Act, 1985 specifies the weight thresholds for small and commercial quantities for narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances:

* **Cannabis (Ganja)**:
  * Small Quantity: **1,000 g (1 kg)** | Commercial Quantity: **20,000 g (20 kg)**
* **Cannabis Resin (Charas / Hashish)**:
  * Small Quantity: **100 g** | Commercial Quantity: **1,000 g (1 kg)**
* **Opium**:
  * Small Quantity: **25 g** | Commercial Quantity: **2.5 kg (2,500 g)**
* **Heroin (Diacetylmorphine)**:
  * Small Quantity: **5 g** | Commercial Quantity: **250 g**
* **Cocaine**:
  * Small Quantity: **2 g** | Commercial Quantity: **100 g**
* **Morphine**:
  * Small Quantity: **5 g** | Commercial Quantity: **250 g**
* **Methadone**:
  * Small Quantity: **2 g** | Commercial Quantity: **50 g**
* **Amphetamine**:
  * Small Quantity: **2 g** | Commercial Quantity: **50 g**
* **Methamphetamine**:
  * Small Quantity: **2 g** | Commercial Quantity: **50 g**
* **MDMA (Ecstasy)**:
  * Small Quantity: **0.5 g** | Commercial Quantity: **10 g**
* **Buprenorphine**:
  * Small Quantity: **1 g** | Commercial Quantity: **20 g**
* **Alprazolam**:
  * Small Quantity: **5 g** | Commercial Quantity: **100 g**
* **Codeine**:
  * Small Quantity: **10 g** | Commercial Quantity: **1,000 g (1 kg)**

question: As per the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Rules, 2022, what new changes have been made in NDPS Forms and what is the complete procedure for filling these forms?
answer:
The Department of Revenue, Government of India, issued the NDPS Rules, 2022 vide G.S.R.
899(E) on 23rd December 2022, under which necessary amendments and modifications have
been made in NDPS forms.
As per the new rules, the procedure for filling NDPS forms is as follows:
1. At the spot, after seizure of narcotic drugs, the Investigating Officer (IO) shall fill NCB-1
(in triplicate) and Form No. 1 (in duplicate).
2. The Investigating Officer (1st or 2nd) shall hand over the accused and seized material
to the SHO at the police station, and a handing over memo shall be prepared.
3. The Station House Officer, after inspection of the seized material, shall re-seal it. He
shall issue a certificate of re-sealing and make a Daily Diary (DD) entry in this regard.
4. Thereafter, the Station House Officer shall hand over the seized property to the Incharge
Malkhana (store room). The Malkhana Munshi shall fill Form No. 2 and make
endorsement on Form No. 1. The Malkhana Incharge shall also issue a receipt.
5. The Malkhana Incharge shall return Form No. 1 (original) and Form No. 2 to the Station
House Officer.
6. The Malkhana Incharge shall maintain a separate register as per Form No. 3.
7. He shall also record the seizure details in Register No. 19.
8. The Station House Officer shall fill Form No. 4 and Form No. 5 and take or send the
seized property to the jurisdictional Magistrate for inventory proceedings.
9. After court orders, the officer producing the case property shall prepare Test Memo
(Form No. 6) in triplicate. One copy shall be sent to FSL along with duplicate samples,
one copy shall remain in the Investigating Officer file, and one copy shall be kept with
the case property in Malkhana. The Test Memo shall be signed by both Station House
Officer and the Magistrate with seal impressions.
10. As per Rule 11, in cases of Opium, Ganja and Charas, two samples of 24 grams each
(original and duplicate) shall be drawn, and for other substances, two samples of 5
grams each shall be drawn.
11. As per Rule 12, sampling shall be done only in plastic packets or glass bottles which
shall be properly sealed.
12. As per Rule 6, case property shall now be stored in a trunk with double lock in the
Malkhana.
13. As per Rule 7, inspection of Malkhana shall be conducted by senior officers.

question: Is videography mandatory when contraband is recovered from a female accused?
answer:
Statutory Position:
Videography of the personal search of a female accused is not expressly mandated under
the bare text of Section 50 of the NDPS Act. Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 mandates audio-
video recording of the search of any place or thing, preparation of the list of articles seized,
and obtaining signatures of witnesses on the seizure memo. However, this provision also
does not specifically mandate audio-video recording of the personal search of any
individual.
Therefore, conducting audio-video recording of the personal search of a female accused is
not legally mandatory.
Practical Guidance:
However, to ensure the dignity, privacy, and safety of the woman, if deemed necessary, the
personal search may be videographed only by a woman police officer through the e-
Sakshya Application, while ensuring strict compliance with legal safeguards and maintaining
the dignity of the female accused.

question: What is the procedure for sampling when a large number of opium plants are found?
answer:
In cases involving a large number of illegally cultivated opium plants, the following procedure
shall be followed:
1. Obtain land details, Khasra number, and ownership information from the village head
(Gram Pradhan) and revenue officials.
2. If the land belongs to the Forest Department, obtain information from the concerned
forest officer and ensure their presence at the spot.
3. Measure the field.
4. Estimate the total number of plants scientifically. For this purpose, select one square
meter plots at different locations in the field, count the plants, uproot or cut them to
determine weight, and calculate the average to estimate total number and weight.
5. Seize the standing crop and collect representative samples of opium or cannabis
plants/twigs through seizure memo.
6. Send a report to the Gazetted Officer under Section 57 of the NDPS Act. If the Gazetted
Officer is present at the spot, no separate report is required.
7. Obtain orders from the Gazetted Officer for attachment and destruction of the crop.
8. Uproot or cut the plants using labour or machinery.
9. Destroy (burn) the plants.
10. Photograph and videograph the entire proceedings and preserve them as evidence.
If the cultivator has been identified and arrested and produced before the court, the crop shall
not be destroyed without court permission. In such cases, the crop shall be stored safely in the
Malkhana and destroyed only after obtaining pre-trial disposal permission under Section 52A
of the NDPS Act.
Note: No separate small or commercial quantity is defined for opium cultivation. This offence
falls under Section 18(c) of the NDPS Act.

question: While operationalising STF Police Stations, how will the territorial jurisdiction of courts and police be determined?
answer:
Section 36A of the NDPS Act, titled “Offences triable by Special Courts”, provides that all
offences punishable with imprisonment exceeding three years shall be triable only by the
Special Court constituted for the area in which the offence has been committed. Where more
than one Special Court exists for the area, the Government may specify the appropriate court.
Accordingly, cases involving commercial and intermediate quantities of contraband shall be
tried by the Special Courts of the district where the seizure has been effected. As regards police
jurisdiction, it was clarified that the police do not have territorial restrictions for investigation of
offences.
